analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for landlords to illegally evict or pressure tenants during a declared national emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced a month before the end of the congressional session, drew no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During a national emergency, such as a pandemic or major disaster, the bill would have made it a federal crime for a landlord to evict a tenant without a court order, or to harass a tenant, cut utilities, change locks, or stop repairs in order to force the tenant out. First offenses could mean up to a year in prison or a fine, repeat offenses up to five years. Tenants could also sue for triple damages and attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, especially those facing eviction pressure during a pandemic or disaster. The bill gave them a federal court order requirement, the ability to sue landlords for three times their damages with attorney's fees paid, and criminal penalties for landlords who use harassment or utility shutoffs instead of the courts.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a landlord from repossessing or attempting to repossess a dwelling without a court order during a national emergency, punishable by up to one year in prison for a first offense and up to five years for repeat offenses [S2] [S3].

Bars landlords from threatening, harassing, or creating a hostile environment to force a tenant out, and from impairing habitability—suspending utilities, changing locks, or refusing repairs—to push a tenant to leave [S2] [S3].
Lets injured tenants sue for injunctive relief, triple damages, and attorneys' fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners, who would face federal criminal exposure and triple-damage lawsuits for evicting or pressuring tenants without a court order during a declared emergency. Honest supporters would also acknowledge that federalizing what states already regulate adds a second layer of enforcement, and that the bill's criminal penalties apply to conduct during any presidentially declared emergency, which some would argue reaches beyond genuine crisis conditions.

drawbacks.text: The bill layers federal criminal penalties on top of state landlord-tenant law, so landlords could face prison time for conduct that states treat as a civil matter, during any presidentially declared emergency under several statutes [S3].

Supporters of current law would argue self-help eviction and habitability rules are already regulated by states, and the bill does not address the underlying problem of unpaid rent during emergencies, only enforcement methods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection—no eviction without a court order, and no harassment or utility shutoffs to force tenants out—is narrow and targets conduct most states already forbid, so the cost to compliant landlords is small. The main design criticism is federal criminal penalties duplicating state law, and the bill never advanced far enough for those questions to be weighed in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in its final month and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on December 7, 2020, in the closing month of the 116th Congress [S1] [S2] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and received no further action [S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without a hearing or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners are better off because the bill died: no federal criminal penalties or triple-damage liability for evictions and tenant-pressure tactics during national emergencies was created. Renters gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; it was his sole sponsorship effort with no cosponsors recruited.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never revealed; the bill's sole sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed federal criminal penalties and triple-damage liability on landlords who evict without a court order or use harassment, lockouts, or utility shutoffs to push tenants out during a declared emergency. Because the bill died, that liability never materialized.
The bill's court-order requirement and penalties would have restricted lockout-based eviction practices and raised the legal risk of aggressive turnover tactics during emergencies.
